lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell me, Carian. What exactly makes you so proud? Why do you expect VIP treatment down here?

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: First of all, Sinopean, my kingdom. I ruled all of Caria, conquered parts of Lydia, took over a few islands, and marched all the way to Miletus, subduing most of Ionia along the way. I was handsome. I was tall. I was a formidable warrior. But the most important thing is my tomb in Halicarnassus. No other dead man has a monument that enormous, or so exquisitely decorated. The horses, the men, sculpted down to the finest detail from the finest marble... you wouldn't easily find a temple that measures up to it. So, yes, I think I'm perfectly justified in putting on a few airs.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Let me get this straight. You're proud of your kingdom, your looks, and the sheer weight of your tomb?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But, my handsome Mausolus, your strength and your looks are entirely gone. [pause] If we brought in a beauty judge right now, I fail to see why your skull would score any higher than mine. We're both bald, we're both bare, we've both got our teeth hanging out, our eyes are missing, and we're entirely lacking in the nose department. As for the tomb and all that expensive marble... I suppose the people of Halicarnassus can show it off to tourists and brag about having a very large building. But *you*, my good man—I don't see what you get out of it. Unless you consider it a privilege to be crushed under a heavier load of rocks than the rest of us.

lines.speaker: Mausolus
lines.text: [genuinely distressed] So it's all useless? You're telling me Mausolus and Diogenes are exactly equal?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Oh, we're not equal, my noble friend. Not at all. Mausolus is going to spend eternity weeping over his earthly memories and his so-called happiness, while Diogenes is going to laugh at him. Mausolus will brag about the tomb his sister-wife built for him in Halicarnassus. Diogenes doesn't even know if his corpse *got* a tomb, because he couldn't care less. He left behind a reputation among thoughtful men for having lived a life of true independence—a monument, you slavish little Carian, built on much firmer ground, and towering significantly higher than yours.
